resources.string: Intellectual Property

This article explains the principles that guide the ownership, use, attribution, and protection of intellectual property associated with Keyboard X. It also describes how users and third-party developers can raise questions about materials that may be protected by applicable law or license terms.
1. Ownership and scope of intellectual property

Intellectual property can include software source code, compiled software, original visual designs, illustrations, icons, written materials, documentation, product names, logos, and other creative elements. The rights associated with each item depend on its origin, the agreements that apply to it, and the laws governing its use. Keyboard X is developed as a native Android keyboard application. Original materials created specifically for the project may be protected by copyright or other applicable intellectual property laws. The precise ownership of a particular item must be determined from its authorship, development history, applicable agreements, and any relevant license. The presence of a file, image, design, or other resource in the application does not, by itself, establish that the project owns every right associated with it. Materials obtained from third parties may remain the property of their respective authors or rights holders. Their use must follow the permissions and conditions that apply to those materials. This page is intended to explain general principles. It does not replace a specific license, written permission, contractual agreement, or legal determination concerning a particular work.
2. Original software and creative materials

Original software and creative materials may include application code, interface arrangements, custom illustrations, original text, documentation, and other work produced for Keyboard X. Protection and permitted use depend on the nature of each work and the applicable law. Unless a separate license or written permission states otherwise, users should not assume that access to the application grants them permission to reproduce, redistribute, commercially exploit, or create derivative works from every original component. Any permission must be interpreted according to its actual terms and applicable law. A feature description, screenshot, public repository, or downloadable build should not be treated as a substitute for checking the license that applies to the specific material. Where the project publishes source code under a separate open-source license, that license governs the components and uses within its stated scope. The terms of one component do not automatically determine the rights applicable to unrelated assets or third-party materials. Before reusing a component, review the relevant repository files, notices, license text, and any additional terms provided by the rights holder. If the applicable permission is unclear, seek clarification before distributing or commercially using the material.
3. Product name, logo, and visual identity

Product names, logos, icons, and other branding elements help users distinguish one product from another. Depending on the circumstances and applicable law, these elements may be protected by trademark, copyright, design rights, or other legal rules. The name Keyboard X and any project branding should be used in a clear and responsible manner. References to the application for identification, compatibility discussions, reviews, tutorials, or factual descriptions should not be presented as evidence of a partnership, sponsorship, certification, or official approval unless that relationship has actually been authorized. If you publish a review, tutorial, comparison, or independent integration involving Keyboard X, describe your relationship with the project accurately. Make it clear when your work is independent, and avoid presenting a modified product as an official release of the original project. This section does not declare that every name or visual element is registered as a trademark. Registration status and the scope of any enforceable rights must be verified separately through reliable records and the relevant jurisdiction.
4. Third-party software and licensed resources

Modern applications may rely on libraries, development tools, fonts, icons, images, or other resources supplied by third parties. Each such component may have its own copyright notice, license, attribution requirement, redistribution condition, or restriction. The terms governing a third-party component remain separate from the terms governing original Keyboard X materials. A permission to use one component does not grant ownership of that component, and it does not automatically authorize uses beyond the applicable license. Anyone redistributing a build, source-code copy, or modified version should review the licenses and notices that apply to the included components. Required notices should be preserved, and any additional obligations should be observed. If a license requires attribution, source availability, inclusion of a license text, or another specific action, follow the exact applicable requirement. The project should maintain accurate notices for the components it actually includes. The presence and terms of a component must be verified against the version being distributed; this article alone is not a complete inventory of third-party software or licenses.
5. Permission, reuse, and redistribution

Before copying, adapting, publishing, or distributing protected material, identify the rights holder and determine whether the intended use is allowed by an applicable license, written permission, or legal exception. Different uses may have different requirements, including attribution, notice preservation, source-code availability, or restrictions on particular forms of distribution. Permission to use a resource for personal reference does not necessarily include permission to incorporate it into another application, sell it, publish a modified version, or use it in promotional materials. Similarly, permission to redistribute software does not automatically grant permission to use a product name or logo in a manner governed by separate rights. When requesting permission, identify the specific material, explain the intended use, describe where and how it will be distributed, and include any relevant links or examples. Keep a record of any permission granted and follow the conditions attached to it. Nothing in this article is intended to remove rights or exceptions that cannot lawfully be excluded. The applicable license and governing law determine the actual scope of permitted use.
6. Modified versions and independent projects

A modified version of an application may contain original project materials, changes made by the modifier, and third-party components. The rights applicable to each part may differ. Permission to modify or redistribute one part does not necessarily extend to every other part of the application. Anyone publishing a modified version should review the relevant licenses, identify material changes where appropriate, preserve required notices, and avoid creating confusion about the source of the release. A modified build should not be described as an official Keyboard X release unless the project has authorized that description. Independent developers should also ensure that their own additions do not improperly reproduce material belonging to others. Where a contribution incorporates code, artwork, text, or another resource from an external source, the contributor should confirm that the material can be used under the proposed distribution terms. These principles are general guidance. The actual rights and obligations for a particular modification depend on the licenses, agreements, project policies, and laws that apply to the materials involved.
7. Respecting the rights of others

Keyboard X aims to treat intellectual property concerns carefully and respectfully. Users, contributors, and other parties should take reasonable steps to ensure that material they submit, publish, or distribute is used with appropriate authorization. If you believe a file, image, name, text, or other resource raises an intellectual property concern, provide enough information to identify the material and explain the concern. Where possible, include the location of the material, the nature of the right involved, your relationship to the rights holder, and relevant supporting documentation. Reports should be factual and specific. A disagreement about a product, a technical issue, or a general concern does not automatically establish an intellectual property violation. Each report requires enough information to understand the issue and determine what further review may be appropriate. Submitting a report does not guarantee a particular outcome. Any action must take account of the information available, the applicable license or law, and the circumstances of the reported material.
8. Reporting a concern

To report a suspected intellectual property issue, contact the support address displayed in the application. Include a clear description of the material concerned, where it appears, why you believe it may infringe a right, and how the support team can contact you if additional information is needed. If you are reporting on behalf of a rights holder, explain your authority to do so. Include relevant links, document references, or other evidence where available, but avoid sending unnecessary sensitive personal information. The initial contact method available in the current version may open an email application and prepare a message for you to review. Opening or preparing an email does not mean the message has been sent or received. You remain responsible for confirming and sending the message through your email application. A report may require clarification before it can be assessed. Please provide accurate information and respond to reasonable follow-up questions where appropriate. Do not use the reporting process to submit abusive, knowingly inaccurate, or unrelated messages.
9. Review and possible responses

After receiving a report, the project may need to review the identified material, the information supplied by the reporter, the applicable license, and any relevant development or publication records. The amount of review possible depends on the information available and the resources of the project. Depending on the circumstances, further information may be requested, a correction may be considered, a relevant notice may be reviewed, or another appropriate step may be evaluated. No particular response time or outcome is guaranteed by this article. A report should be assessed on its specific facts rather than on assumptions about ownership or intent. Where ownership, authorization, or legal obligations are disputed, additional documentation or qualified legal advice may be necessary. This description is not a formal notice-and-takedown procedure and does not replace any process required by applicable law. Any legally required process, deadline, or remedy takes precedence over this general explanation.
10. Accuracy and limitations

This article provides general information about intellectual property principles associated with software and digital materials. It is not legal advice and should not be relied upon as a determination of ownership, infringement, licensing status, or available remedies in a specific dispute. The rights applicable to a particular item may depend on its author, creation date, source, license, contractual history, and jurisdiction. Some uses may be permitted by law even without individual permission; other uses may require authorization. Those questions must be assessed according to the facts and applicable legal rules. The project may revise this page as the application, its included components, licensing arrangements, or support procedures change. A revised article should not be interpreted as changing the terms of a separate license or agreement unless that instrument is validly amended in accordance with its own requirements.
11. Contact and further information

For questions about intellectual property associated with Keyboard X, use the support contact displayed within the application. Describe your question clearly and identify the relevant material or repository location when possible. Before relying on a particular license or permission, consult the actual license text or written authorization. Before taking action in a legal dispute, consider obtaining advice from a qualified professional familiar with the applicable jurisdiction. This article is intended to make the project's approach easier to understand and to provide a practical starting point for questions about ownership and permitted use. The rights and obligations for any specific material remain governed by the relevant facts, licenses, agreements, and applicable law.
